utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue with the evidence now. I remind you that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, we -- we're going again today and I'm afraid we have a long way to go. Again, let me just remind you that I'm going to try to ask questions that you can answer easily and quickly. If you don't understand them, let me know and I'll rephrase them, and let's see if we can get through this as quickly as possible. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, could you make sure your voice is directed towards the microphones, please. We'll have them adjusted slightly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday when -- right near the end of your testimony, Mr. Hannis showed you a document that was some kind of an interview report either from the OSCE or the ICG. And you told us that you recognised it, that it had your name on it, and that in fact you had signed it. And it's about that report right now that I want to ask you just a couple of questions. In the supplemental information sheet that we were provided by the Prosecutor, that indicates that you told them here on the 28th of August that that statement you gave to the -- to the Crisis Group or to the OSCE, that you were exhausted when you gave that statement - correct - or that interview?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would I be correct in assuming that you're telling us you were exhausted when you gave that interview so that we would understand that some of the things you said in there may not be correct, that you said them just because you were exhausted?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the things you said during that interview were to the best of your knowledge at that time the truth about what you'd observed and what happened?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as I know --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as I know, that interview was the first account that you gave to any outside party, any other organisation about the experiences you'd had in Kosovo and getting out of Kosovo. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And apparently this statement was given like maybe the day you came to Macedonia or a day later. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the things that's -- that's contained in that is the interviewer says, and to be fair to you I think it's important that you hear exactly what the interviewer said. "Villagers heard soldiers speaking Russian." Did you tell the interviewer that you had heard soldiers speaking Russian or that other villagers told you that they had heard soldiers speaking Russian?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you didn't notice this when you signed that interview form?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know anything about any of the soldiers that were in your village ever speaking Russian?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how that got in this interview report if you hadn't said it to the interviewer?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking with the three officers, the Serbian soldiers and his colleagues, the other officers, referred to him by the name of Russ, not the population, but the soldiers called him Russ, meaning Russian in Albanian. He was a Serbian officer, but a nickname by which he was known was Russ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Also in this same interview report, you're talking about the events of 6th April of 1999. According to the interviewer you said that there were a line of about 3.000 people standing on the main road who were threatened at gunpoint by approximately 100 paramilitaries. Is that what you told the interviewer?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: According to this report you told the interviewer that at about 2.00 in the afternoon on the 6th of April, you left your village and went toward Bujanovac. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So of the things that I've mentioned that were in that report, they were all wrong except that one that we just talked about; true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one is correct. The first, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you don't remember or they're wrong? I think you told me it was wrong that the villagers heard someone speaking Russian and wrong that the group was threatened by a hundred paramilitaries at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to make an explanation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked only with the officers, with the Serbian officers. On the western side of the village, however, there were Serbian soldiers who looted and raided the village. Nobody said that they spoke Russian; they did speak Serbian. As to what you are putting to me, that 100 soldiers or so looted the village, that is true. This occurred only on the western side of the village, but the eastern side of the village was left intact; this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to the first statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, that was the statement of 25 April 1999. And I'm going to refer to that along with some of the testimony you gave here yesterday. At page 6 of yesterday's testimony, beginning at line 21, you were telling us about the 6th of April in your village, Prilepnica. You were at your mother's house, and you -- you told us yesterday, quoting: "I heard gun- fire from all sides in Prilepnica." Do you remember saying that in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you were asked by Mr. Hannis what you did when you heard that gun-fire, and you said this, quoting again your testimony: "For the moment I was stunned, and after talking with some of my relatives I decided to go in the direction of the southern part of the village from where the gun-shot was heard." Now, the first question I have about that is: You say you walked toward where the gun-shot was heard. Did you mean to say that you'd only heard one gun-shot and not multiple gun-shots?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shots came from all sides, and there were many shots, not just one. And I and some others set out in the direction of the south, which is at the entrance to the village because this is where most of the shots came from. And in this situation, people of course are scared. And my friend stopped somewhere and I continued my way along. After walking 5 or 600 metres I ran into the first soldier with the two hostages that I mentioned, Nazim Xhelil and Shefik Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us now that the villagers were afraid. You weren't afraid since you walked absolutely in the direction where the most shooting was happening, so you were not afraid. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was too scared, but someone had to go and talk to those people, and I found the way to talk with them, but as to fear, I was very much afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP of 25 April 1999, and it's at paragraph 9 of that statement, you told the interviewer then, back in 1999, shortly after these events, that when you walked into the village that you saw two soldiers who had arrested two villagers. In your testimony here yesterday, at page 7, line 5, you said it was only one soldier. Now, can you tell us how it would have been two soldiers in April of 1999 and one soldier yesterday? How did that change happen?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several soldiers, sir, but near the hostages there was only one, the one who was threatening them with his gun. But the other soldiers were standing some 10 or 15 metres away. I can't give you the exact figure, but there were many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, that's my fault. I wasn't specific enough with the question I asked you. In your statement of April of 1999, a statement which you told me yesterday that you signed after it had been read to you, the exact language of that statement regarding what you said is this: "I saw two soldiers in Serbian army uniforms who had arrested two villagers." Yesterday, describing that same incident, you saw one soldier who had arrested two villagers. My question is: Why did that change between April of 1999 and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I remembered better how many soldiers were there, for the moment I didn't remember the soldier that was a little bit further away. What mattered to me was the conversation I had with -- with one of the soldiers. So I gave the answer, thinking of the person I talked to because that was the question: With whom did I talk? And I said I talked with one soldier, and the question was not how many soldiers I saw, at least this is the way I understood the question put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. At -- at one point you said that these villagers were being held for ransom. What was the ransom demand that was being made?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a reference to the ransom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's -- if you don't get it now, Mr. Hannis, we'll get it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking for it now because I remember hostage and not ransom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I failed to make a note about it. I know it's there. It's in the -- it's in the transcript from yesterday, page 8, it looks like it's line 19. The soldier who was holding the two people ransom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you said they were being held for ransom? What was the ransom they were being held for?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything about being held for ransom. My point was they being - they'd been kept hostages. They were kneeling on the road, and the gun was pointed at them. That's what I meant by "ransom."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they were hostages for what purpose? What was it that was being demanded for their release?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, sir, Nazim Xhelili, when he saw me walking there, he addressed me in a kind of loud voice: Come here, come over here Hoxh because this is imam, I think. I don't know, they wanted someone to talk to, and as to your question why did they hold them hostages, I don't know. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you used the word "hostage," not me, and maybe if you had tended to use the prisoner, would that be more accurate? Rather than being held hostages they were being held prisoner, because you said they had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used the word "prisoner." The meaning of the word "prisoner" for me is when somebody is kept in a prison and not held at gun-point in the street kneeling on the ground. That's the means of hostage, or ransom - call it what you want - for me. I don't find any other word to use to describe that scene. If there is any other word you might wish to use, you can go ahead and use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that permission. Do you know why these two villagers had been arrested by these two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, when the Serbian soldier entered the village at around 8.00 they went into the villagers' homes and had found people there. They had caught 100 or 150 villagers and shoved them in a house. They had taken these two that I saw with them and brought them to the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what -- what had they done, what crime had they committed, that they were arrested? Why were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were beaten and brought to that place by the soldiers. As to the reason why, it's the soldiers who know that; I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told us yesterday that in addition to the soldier or soldiers that were holding these two people, that there were 12 or 15 other soldiers nearby. That's page 8, line 4. And then you were asked this by Mr. Hannis at line 16: "Did you see any kind of insignia or badges or markings of rank on any of these uniforms?" And your answer was this, quoting you: "No, no. They didn't have any rankings that I saw." How about badges, did you see any badges?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember to have seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that 1999 statement that you gave to the Prosecutor's office, which you must have had a chance to review before you started testifying here yesterday, you said that these people were wearing "olive-drab uniform of the regular Serbian army, black beret, with a badge with semicircles similar to Srpska Garda." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't said this. I never mentioned any markings or any black beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that that was not in your statement of April of 1999, or will you take my word for it that it was in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first sentence that the colour was olive-green-grey uniform, it's true; as to what they were wearing on their hats or the markings or insignia, this I never said. So it's partially true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that that language is in your statement that you read and signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't read it, Your Honour, it was read to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was read to you and then you signed it. Would it surprise you that language was contained in that statement which you said was true to the best of your recollection just a few days after this event?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you talk about berets, no matter what colour they were or any rankings or insignia, that is not my sentence, neither at that time nor now. That would certainly surprise me if you put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there a copy of this statement that could be given to the witness so that he could look at -- give him the B/C/S because I know where he can find it in the B/C/S and he can read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can give it to me in Serbo-Croatian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I said. I should have said "Serbo- Croatian." We call it "B/C/S" here for convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's P2288, if you want to put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understood it was not in the system, Your Honour, but if it's in the system --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that not the interview that the witness was referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. This is the one with the OTP. The one yesterday was the ICG --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, the 25th of April one you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have a copy. We've given it to him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think you're going to find it --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English, what I have in front of me. I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know why you got English. That won't help you, will it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should give it to me in Albanian or in Serbo-Croatian, that I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're trying to find one in Serbo-Croatian for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have it here if the usher will come get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a full paragraph there near the bottom of the page, the 12th paragraph. You should find in there that it says that you said: "... black beret with a badge with semicircles similar to Srpska Garda." Let me know if you find that.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it even indicates that the interviewer showed you some kind of a badge that was similar to the one that you claimed to have seen, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The emblems or the caps that are mentioned here was shown to me - - were in a -- on a picture. And the question asked of me was: Do you recognise these uniforms or helmets? I said: Yes, but I didn't mean that they were the ones that belonged to the soldiers that I mentioned. It's a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So when that was read back to you so you'd have a chance to correct any misunderstandings, you just missed that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that assumes it was read back to him correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we have to assume that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we not entitled to assume that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he already indicated previously in his testimony that he had a problem with that interpreter not being very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was read the statement in Albanian at that time by the interpreter, who was from Macedonia. And I never saw it after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are matters for -- for submission and assessment at the end of the day, there's nothing wrong with the question being posed on the assumption that the reading back was accurate. If you want to prove otherwise in due course, Mr. Hannis, it will be open to you to prove that the Prosecution witness statements were not being read back accurately. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was only because in this case he had made a specific reference to this interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Hannis, but we're going to get this repeatedly, I suspect, in light of the way in which these statements were taken. Carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for record purposes, I'll remind Your Honours that this is the second time that we've had that kind of reaction that the statement must have been read back improperly. The first time the claim was it was read back too fast, and if we can't rely on these statements -- on these averments at the end of these statements that are signed under oath that it was read back to him and he can understand it, then what can we rely on? If that's going to be the Prosecutor's position, then I don't know that we can ever rely on a 92 bis statement or any other statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult for it to be the Prosecutor's position, Mr. Ackerman, if he's presenting these statements taken by his office and then leading the evidence. So if he wishes to undermine them, then he'll need to take steps to see that that's done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was trying to refer not to a black beret, but I'm trying to refer to this badge with semicircles similar to Srpska Garda. Now, I find it hard to believe that that would be a mistake going into your statement, that someone would put in a badge with semicircles similar to Srpska Garda if you hasn't said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that mischaracterises his testimony. He was asked if he recognised it and he said yes, he recognised it. He said the mistake was them reporting it was worn to one of the soldiers he was talking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he has given evidence, Mr. Ackerman, that all he was asked was whether he recognised what was shown to him and he said he did and he didn't relate that to the particular soldiers that he's been giving evidence about or about whom he was talking about in his statement. Now, that's his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that -- that tends to conflict with the statement, and let me read this to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, of course it conflicts with the statement. You may never square the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may not, Your Honour. I'll give up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has to be borne in mind here, Mr. Hannis, is that -- Mr. Ackerman, is that Mr. Hannis may be content at the end of the day with the explanations that the witness gives, no matter frustrated you may turn out to be because of the results that this exercise produces. On the other hand, there may be more acute circumstances in which the disagreement is such that the Prosecutor has to make his mind up whether he concedes that the witness is telling two different tales or whether he seeks to advance an explanation which can only be advanced if further evidence is called. So these are difficult things to make final judgements on at this stage, but this is one good example probably of a situation where the Chamber would have to evaluate the context in which both the statement itself and the evidence were given and all of the surrounding circumstances and assess whether what we are hearing in court is a reliable account.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll move on to another area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what -- yes, I'm reminded that this particular document is not in the system. Now, it may be you wish to introduce it and now would be the time, I suppose, to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We tried quite hard to get it into the system last night, Your Honour, and failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We got all the rest of them in, but for some reason a communication problem of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all do you wish to introduce it into evidence here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case we'll take the hard copy and give it an IC number for the moment in anticipation that you'll tidy the record up by introducing the electronic version in all the languages in which it exists, and noting that that is the equivalent or the same as IC whatever the number is given to it, so we don't get confused by the same document having two different references.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can say it will go in as 4D10. Is that correct? I think our last document is 4D9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it's in the system as 4D5, identified as transcript of handwritten notes. So maybe it is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think that's a matter for you to resolve and you can sort it out with the registry rather than do it here. What we will do for the moment is give the document the witness has been reading from an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC32, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's carry on with the cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Your Honour, I promise I'll get more familiar with e-court and these problems won't occur in the future. I apologise for this little problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you are talking to the partially sighted, so I understand the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember describing this soldier that was holding - - or one of the soldiers that was holding these two people, describing his uniform as having a bandanna on his head?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you describe that bandanna? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a black colour bandanna, tied on the back of his head, nothing specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. At one point fairly early in this conversation you had with soldiers, they indicated to you that they wanted to search the village and you told them that they were welcome to search the village if they wanted to, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk with the soldiers but with a soldier in singular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The same question I just asked you without the S on the end of soldier. Did you talk to that soldier about KLA hiding in the village and you told him they were welcome to search the village if they wanted to? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not welcomed, but he ordered me to move out the village, and his excuse was that the KLA add emerged in the village. If necessary, I can say in B/C/S his words, I can quote him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to. I want you to answer my question, and I'm going to tell you where to look. I want you to look in the statement that you have in front of you on page 3, paragraph 2. And you should find language to this effect. He had asked you about KLA, weapons, and terrorists. You said this: "I told him that we had nothing of the kind, but they were welcome to search if they wanted." Now, is that what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to them: There is no KLA, there are no weapons. I didn't say: You're welcome. I told them: It is your right to search the village, you can do that. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now my question is: Do you see that language in your statement that says you told them they were welcome to search if they wanted? Do you see it there in paragraph 3 on page 2?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this paragraph is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, paragraph 2 -- page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them that there is nothing of that sort in our village, but that they can search it if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It hasn't been translated correctly. It's not that I said: You're welcome to search. I did not say that they were welcome; I just said if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's an interesting difference, and this is a -- this is a statement that you told us yesterday was read over to you in Albanian and that you signed it, swearing that upon your honour and conscience that it accurately reflected your interview, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree, Mr. Hannis. Please move on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These two soldiers or one soldier, as you said yesterday, eventually took you to someone that they called the commander, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I informed my people, using the loud-speaker from the mosque, I met with this soldier, then we walked together for 200 metres. And in the end of the village, there were the three officers or their command, about 150 to 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you probably could have just said "yes" to my question and we'd move along a little faster. Try to do that, if you can. According to your statement, this commander told you: The village is going to be bombed by NATO, that they're going to lay mines in the village, it would be dangerous for you to stay there, and you would have to leave. True?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What partly not? I'm just quoting from your statement mostly. What's wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information that this village would be shelled by NATO. We will prevent that by all means available to us. And what you just said in Albanian, how it was translated to me, it is a little bit difficult -- different. So these are two different things: We have been informed and: They are going to shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And you were told it would be dangerous to stay there and you would have to leave; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what they supposed would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you testified yesterday, page 18, line 24, you told us that: "They said," I assume that's this commander, "that they were going to mine the dam as well as the village and that that order came from above and it was necessary for them to carry it out." Now, which one of them was it that told you that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three officers that were there as well as the officer who was present when we were encircled in Gjilan at the hospital, they used the same sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So all three of them said that. Did they say it altogether or separately?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all of them together, separately. First one of them said it, when the three officers were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which one? Who said it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 6th of April, I don't know their names. I've only described the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were talking to three officers and you told us: "They said this ... " Did all of them say it or did just one of them say it? "They" doesn't describe anybody? Who said it? The middle one? The left one? The right one? Is it just one?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the one that also said: The order came from above and it was necessary for them to carry it out; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mainly spoke to the one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the one that said what I just quoted to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never mentioned this mining of the dam or the order coming from above in any of the prior statements you gave regarding these matters, did you? Yesterday was the first time we'd heard that. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, yes, because I don't remember if I mentioned this or not when I gave my first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you had a chance to review your first statement after you came to The Hague for your testimony in this case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had the chance, and as I said I made some corrections. There were some technical mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did -- we're going to get to those. You didn't see this language in that statement, did you, because you never told anybody this? It never made it into any of your OTP statements, did it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was the first time that you told somebody from the OTP about the mining of the dam and the order that came from above? When was the first time you told a representative of the OTP that story?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been on the 19th, 18th or 19th of April when an OSCE representative from Switzerland interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your contention that you gave this account that early; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the questions were yes or no questions. I was asked to give brief answers, just to answer their questions and not to narrate all the events that had happened, just to be specific in my answers. So as I was telling the story, it happened that he would interrupt me and said: It's enough. You don't have to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, is that true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- can you give me a moment, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you now able to tell us definitely that the statement was given to the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first statement that I gave was to the OSCE. I also have the business card of the person who interviewed me; it is with me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of that person, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it is in the supplemental information, the name of the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on, hold on, Mr. Shaqiri. This is -- that is information I don't have. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you may not have received the supplemental information because we were leading him as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. So if -- I take it then that this is not information covered by any form of privilege?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Would you give me the name then, please, Mr. Shaqiri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thomas Hunecke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you spell the second name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the usher can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, H-u-n-e-c-k-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about when you were interviewed by Catherine Driguet on did you tell her this story about the mining of the village and the order from above?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did tell her the story, but it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now about when you talked to Annette Murtagh in June 2001, did you tell her that story about the mining of the dam and the order from above?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how about when you talked with the Prosecutor on 28 August 2006, talked to Keith Scully and Irina Dragulev, did you tell them the story about the mining of the dam and the order from above?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time you mentioned, mostly I corrected these technical mistakes. The full statement is the second one in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think I've managed to confuse you. You talked with the Prosecutor in February of 2002, an interviewer by the name of Jan Pfundheller and that is this one of corrections of mistakes. The one on the 28th of August when you talked to Keith Scully and Irina Dragulev, is what they call a supplemental information sheet. This isn't a correction of mistakes, this is additional information that you provided that wasn't in any of your statements and I'm just wondering if you told them during that interview that you had on the 28th of August about the mining of the dam and the order from above?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to the characterisation of the supplemental information --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Shaqiri, I'm listening to Mr. Hannis for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think if you have a look at the supplemental information, you'll see it is supplemental information as well as corrections of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do see some -- there is a few mistake corrections in here, maybe three in 27 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember if you mentioned it then?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, during your testimony about this event in your village on the 6th of April yesterday at page 19, line 1 of the transcript - and maybe I should explain something to you before I go any further. Do you understand that every word that you say is being recorded and that that is given to us in writing so that we can see today exactly what you said yesterday. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 19, line 1 yesterday, talking about these soldiers, you said: "They did not threaten to kill us, no, they didn't do this." Now, I wonder how you reconcile that with testimony that you gave just before that, that they told you that they would kill you first, that you'd be the first to be executed?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may not be clear to you, but there is an explanation. The officers whom I went to see, they threatened me. It's not the soldiers who threatened me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But those officers did not threaten to kill villagers apparently; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only the officers who were on the road, and they had nothing to do with other villagers; they just spoke with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to -- I want to back up a little bit to paragraph -- to page 14, paragraph 16 of your testimony yesterday, and that's where you talk about this soldier nicknamed Russ. And you told us yesterday -- you're not going to find it in that statement. I'm looking at the transcript. You told us about this soldier nicknamed Russ. And you said Russ told you that an order has come from Belgrade that people must be moved out of Prilepnica. Now, did you ever say anything about Russ and him telling you that there was an order from Belgrade in any of your prior statements? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did. And do you claim that you mentioned Russ before, in statements you'd given before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My signature and my notes, I gave a statement in handwriting, in my own handwriting, and I don't see it exist. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's interesting. Does anybody know where that is? Your Honour, I wonder if the Prosecutor knows where the statement he gave in his own handwriting is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who did you give that statement to?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To these here, to the office, to the OTP office. I gave them my handwritten statement where I have written in detail what had happened with my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's never been provided to us. I'd like to know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're checking on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll see the heading on the statement -- this is the 25th of April one, yeah, it's referred to as handwritten notes of interview, but that would suggest, I imagine, the handwriting of the interviewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it appears it's -- it's transcribed at -- it was disclosed on the 27th of May, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't look as though that's what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I see -- I see a document that appears to be a handwritten document in French that appears to be a statement from him on the 25th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, the interviewer was French.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that may be her transcript -- her handwritten transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, when was it that you gave the handwritten statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was after we returned to Kosova sometime in July or August 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's as close as you're getting at the moment, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen that handwritten statement since you turned it over to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the person you gave it to?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an Albanian lawyer from Gjilan. I'll check if I have his business card here. His name is Masar Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I see that card, please, Mr. Shaqiri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't find the card, but I know his name. He is an Albanian from Gjilan. He collected photographs and other statements, so it was handed over to Masar Morina, a lawyer from Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What had he to do with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He cooperated with the ICTY office in Pristina, and everything that he had collected he submitted it to the ICTY field office in Pristina. This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday during your testimony, it's page 17 of the transcript in line 5, you talked about the soldiers firing in the air and how that was creating a danger and how one of the soldiers was, in fact, injured by a ricochet from one of the bullets; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell that for the first time yesterday or is that also contained in your statements?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned in my statement as well that an Albanian was wounded, and this I didn't mention yesterday because I forgot to mention it. There were two people who were injured, an Albanian and this soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you claim to have had that in a statement that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a name is there Nexhmedin Kazizi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that in the handwritten one that you gave to this fellow, Morina, or whatever his name is?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be in other statements as well, this Nexhmedin Kazizi, but the Serbian soldier, I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you claim in the statements you gave to the OTP that you talked about this Serbian soldier being wounded, injured; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would surprise you if that wasn't if your statements, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be somewhere in my statements, in one of these three statements. I must have mentioned it with the interviewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I take it there was a time prior to yesterday that you had an opportunity to meet with Mr. Hannis to talk about your testimony in this trial. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how long you met with Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps for an hour or two. I didn't actually look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Hannis when you met with him about the -- the order coming from Belgrade and the mining of the dam and the Albanian and the Serbian being injured by the shooting in your village? Did you tell Mr. Hannis about these things when he interviewed you, when he met with you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you told us about a person named Goroljub Denic?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goroljub Denic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Goroljub Denic, and you did this page 18, line 10 of your transcript yesterday. You told us that he was a Serb from your village who was part of the army, in fact that he was part of the army that had begun shooting in your village at 8.00 that morning. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you put a group together to go to Gjilan to talk to the chief of police to try to keep from having to leave your village, you told us that he went with you, he was part of your group that was going to go beg the chief to change the order. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did come with us because there was no other chance for us going to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was dressed in his army uniform and carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course he had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I represent to you that none of this is in any statement that I've seen that you gave to the OTP. Do you believe that it was in statements that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask if you could request counsel to refer to paragraph 5 of the witness's 25 April 1999 statement and see if perhaps there is a reference that may pertain to that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, the Goran Denic name had been mentioned, Your Honour, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what uniform he was wearing and whether he was carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was referring to the trip to Gjilan with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't mention that in any of your statements, did you, that he went with you to Gjilan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met him only to go to Gjilan, for no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you have to meet him to go to Gjilan? What was the purpose in that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when you are threatened with death and when you feel endangered, you try to find someone who can help you, someone you can rely on, through whom you can contact someone with authority who can help you save your life and the lives of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for clarification of that reference to paragraph 5 of the statement. In that previous statement, Mr. Shaqiri, you make mention of two persons, Negovan Denic and Goran Denic. Now, are they different people from Goroljub Denic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are from a family in my village. I said earlier that there were five or six Serbian households in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what I'm trying to clarify is whether Goran Denic is the same person as the one you yesterday referred to Goroljub Denic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goroljub Denic, Goran Denic, and -- it's the same person, Goce Denic also, they are three names describing the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us in that statement, it's page 3, line 29, statement of April 25, 1999, you said that there were about a hundred soldiers around the command post and that they were all dressed the same way. Do you remember that? It's page 4, paragraph 5 of the statement you have there, if you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. There were about 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All dressed the same way?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I saw were dressed in the same way, in this olive-green- grey uniform with some exceptions, few exceptions, like Goran and the officer were wearing camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- and then you said in the very next sentence, if you look at it: "Some of them had black scarves tied around their heads and others wore black berets." So were they all dressed the same way or not?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they passed before me, those who came from the western side, some of them were wearing scarves, some berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said about these 100 soldiers that they were all dressed the same way, that wasn't correct, was it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And should we take it that the other things you've told us yesterday and in your statements are approximations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You finally left the village. I want to go to the time when you have left the village and you're on the trip away from the village and you pass two roadblocks that you said were manned by soldiers. Serb military, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the first one you told us yesterday, page 24, 6, was at Kmetofc --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how far is that from Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take -- as the crow flies, it's 500 metres. But if you walk, you have to go to the well, go back to Kmetofc, and it takes about 4 or 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's very close, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's close. Kmetofc village is divided by -- from the road by 50, 60 Serbian families, and from our village as the crow flies it's not more than 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, you went there with your group of people from your village because you had been told by these soldiers that you were required to leave because of an order from above; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because of the order and because we felt endangered. We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you got to that place at Kmetofc, there was a roadblock there, a check-point there, where you encountered these Serb military that we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you told us yesterday at 24, line 12: "The police looked at the convoy of people and didn't do anything, but the soldiers, the army soldiers, stopped us." And then you told us that soldier asked you why you were leaving and where you were going; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told that soldier that you were leaving on orders of the army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us this soldier, quoting your language: "Showed surprise, and he told me: 'One hears everything these days.'" Correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So a soldier who is by the crow flies 500 metres from your village, 5 kilometres by road, apparently had no knowledge whatsoever about any order from above that you should leave the village; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, didn't -- didn't his remark make you a bit suspicious about whether there were really orders from above that you should leave, that this soldier so very near the village didn't even know about it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a regular army there, as I said earlier. They had left the barracks and were stationed in Kmetofc village. In the past, we never had any problems, even though we have used that road several times. Whether he knew or not, this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And both of the check-points that you passed through that day on your way, the army personnel you encountered didn't bother you in any way, did they?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, not at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement you gave in June of 2001 you said this: "As we passed these two roadblocks, nothing happened to us, no documents where money was demanded from us, and I had not heard of anyone making a complaint about any type of ill treatment." True?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, and I am repeating that it's a fact that they didn't do anything to us. They just escorted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I would like the registrar to put exhibit IC29 up on the screen and I'll get to it in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you reached Bujanovac, the police told you they had orders to tell you to return to your homes, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they told you that nothing would happen to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't that make you even more suspicious, that the people who told you to leave in the first place didn't have any authority to do so?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see the map on your screen, IC29?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, as you acknowledged yesterday, you weren't turned around until you'd actually crossed the border and entered Serbia proper; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you had no difficulty whatsoever crossing that border, did you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an administrative boundary. There were no people there. I explicitly stated: It's an administrative boundary, it's not a border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's all -- everything's part of Serbia and Montenegro, now Serbia, but that was the line between Kosovo and the rest of Serbia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was only a sign board, Serbia and Montenegro, and the other side writes Kosova. You can see to this day, it's in English. And even to this day there's no one there; it's not manned by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there actually a sign that said "Serbia and Montenegro" at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the sign "Kosova" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that there would be a sign that said "Kosovo," but was there one in reverse that said "Serbia and Montenegro"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I didn't look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm surprised to hear this referred to as a border, you see, and I don't think in fact you do refer to it. You simply see it as a municipality boundary, which is the edge of the -- which is the edge of Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There has always been a sign board right in Kosova when you enter Kosova and Serbia on the reverse side when you enter Serbia. The road, per se, finishes and there is a bridge that divides Serbia from Kosova. It's an administrative, as we call it, boundary, municipality boundary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm surprised to hear about the sign, but we'll perhaps hear more of that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a possibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After being turned around by the police, many of the people went back to the village and I think you told us yesterday that you spent the night in Dobercan before you returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you then go back the next day?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement of June 2001 to the OTP you -- you said that: "All but two families had returned to the village ... " And then in 5 February of 2002, your statement then when you made corrections, you corrected this and said: "There were more than two families that didn't return." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to explain something. When we went on our way to Serbia, two families returned to Ternovc, went to Ternovc. The others, we went to other villages. I went to Dobercan myself. About these two families, I knew, but that night some families returned to our village. But most of them remained in other villages. We were spread out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was true up until the 13th of April when you left again or did all of those families come back by the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't leave on the 13th of April. On the 13th, the officers that I mentioned earlier came to give us the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my mistake. You left the next day, I think on the 14th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was: Had all of the families returned by the 13th -- the 14th? Were they all back then or was there still some that hadn't returned?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some who didn't return. The two families I mentioned. Other families had left in the meantime, but about 90 per cent of the village was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serbs that lived in the village, had they returned?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs didn't leave the village. It was only the Roma -- the Roma villagers that left, along with the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told us yesterday on questioning by Mr. Hannis that the village was completely empty, that wasn't true. There were still some people living there after you left the first time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the 6th of April, until the 7th when we returned that -- at that time there were very few families that remained in the village. This is what I meant, not the entire week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that and maybe make it a little bit clearer here in just a moment? Your Honour, I'm going to a -- basically a new subject right now. Would you like to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be convenient, and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Shaqiri, during your testimony yesterday, Mr. Hannis asked you about the second time that you left the village, and this is page 40, line 19 after yesterday's transcript. He asked: "How many people were in the convoy this time," the second time? And you said: "The same as the first time." I only want to ask you this: If more than two families had failed to return to your village from the first time, who were the extra people that were in the convoy the second time, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village, there were people who came to our village from other places during that week. And then there were the people of Kosac village. So there were even more than the first time during the second time. I'm telling you that we left at the border 518 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you about the people from Kosac. I'm asking you how many people left your village, how many people were in that convoy, and you told Mr. Hannis it was the same as the first time. And I think you've answered that. I think you said some extra people came to your village and made up for the difference. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Hannis asked you about the condition of your village after you returned from that first time you left. You came back to the village and you told him that while you were gone, the houses had been looted and raided, that's at page 32, line 6. He then asked you this: "Did you have occasion to talk with any of the villagers who had stayed behind on the 6th?" And you said: "Yes." Right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then Mr. Hannis said: "Were they able to tell you anything about how this had happened, about how the looting had occurred, or about who had done it?" And then you described the looting and what parts of the village were affected. And then he said: "And did they tell you who had done it?" And you said: "We all knew who did it." He then pointed out that you were several kilometres away at the time and what he really wanted to know was what the villagers who stayed behind had told you about what did it. And at that point you then said: "There weren't any because everybody had left the village. No one stayed behind." So you went from telling him: Yes, you had talked to the villagers who stayed behind to no one stayed behind. Now, those can't both be true, can they?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to make an explanation, sir. I was talking about the villagers who remained there during the night, whom the police returned in the village for the night. There wasn't anyone during the day. Those families that returned to the village on the 6th of April at night, they spent the night in the village, whereas we spent the night in other villages. This is what I meant by that. But when we left the village during the day, not a single one remained; but during night, there were a few families that returned. So there is a difference between the day and the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So when Mr. Hannis said to you, line 6, page 32: "Did you have occasion to talk with any of the villagers who had stayed behind on the 6th?" You thought he was talking about those that had come back the first day; is that what you're telling us, that you understood it to mean the villagers that came back the day before you did and not the ones who stayed behind on the 6th? Is that what you're telling us now, that that's the question you were answering?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have misunderstood it. I didn't stay in the village on the 6th. I talked with the people who had spent the night in the village when I returned there on the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there were villagers who stayed in the village the night of the 6th that you talked to after you came back?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked with them on the next day, as I explained, because on the 6th I was not in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then I guess it was not correct when you told Mr. Hannis a little later that: "Everyone had left the village and no one stayed behind." You're now telling us some people did stay behind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what this evidence so far amounts to. It amounts to saying that some were returned by the evening of the 6th. One of the problems about this line also, Mr. Ackerman, is that it all starts with a question that probably Mr. Hannis should never have asked because it presupposes evidence from the witness that certain people did stay behind. And I don't know if, prior to Mr. Hannis's question, there was such a statement from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're into -- well, there comes a time in even the most focused of cross-examinations when we feel that the law of diminishing returns had begun to kick in. I wonder if we've reached that stage in this cross-examination or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you highlights yet to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are highlights yet to come, Your Honour. I haven't even gotten to the next trip out of the village, and no one wants to stop this cross-examination more than me because I'm very tired and it's very hard for me to stand on my feet this long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We've got you back in the village now. You went back on the 7th, and just to remind you, you told us you had been told by the police that they had orders from the Gjilan chief to return you home and told you that no harm would come to you. And what you told us yesterday about that, page 30, line 13: "I felt good to hear such words, and I informed my people, telling them to pass the news to all the convoy and return to our homes." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was on the 6th of April at the check-point when we crossed the border to Serbia. The police of Kamenice told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And then Mr. Hannis asked you about life in the village after you had returned, after you had been told that no harm would come to you. He asked if life was normal. And this is the answer you gave, it's on page 34, beginning with line 4, you said: "No, the life was no longer normal. Every citizen tried his or her best to contact people with authority who were of Serb nationality to avoid moving out from the village because there was no reason for us to move. Subsequently, on the 9th and 10th of April, we stood guard duty together with the police from the town." So in spite of these comforting words from the police that made you feel so good, somehow you knew that they were coming back on the 13th to throw you out again? And if you knew that, how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We hoped that we would never be forced to leave the village and that we thought that the 6th of April event was a mistake on the part of the army, but we were disillusioned when we saw the order repeated on the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, but in your answer to Mr. Hannis you're saying that people from the village were contacting Serbs in authority to avoid moving out. I mean, what -- how could that be? What threat was there to move out at that point right after you came back on the 7th and the 8th and the 9th and the 10th? There were no soldiers there telling you to move out. Why are they contacting Serbs to avoid moving out, or is this just made up? Did you make it up?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't make it up at all, sir. After the beating, the looting, the raids that occurred on the 6th of April, we were no longer the same, of course. And we wanted by all means to feel safe and to make sure that this thing didn't happen again, and I didn't mean each and every one in the village. I told you, we are surrounded by seven Serbian villages, and we have always had good relations with them. I told you that my family has been Hoxha for 150 years, and we haven't had any cases of murder, either committed by Albanians or by Serbs. So I take pride at my people and at our neighbours. But the fear of having again what happened on the 6th of April, which was something uncivilised, amoral, in our eyes, we thought that by contacting someone we knew in Gjilan, in the militia, in the police, and other places, we would make sure we continued the same life as before. Because, as I said, life couldn't be as normal as it was before. Even if you were there yourself, I'm sure you would have done the same. We were very much afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told us yesterday about life being no longer normal, when you said to us: "Every citizen tried his or her best to contact people with authority who were of Serb nationality," that was an exaggeration? It really wasn't every citizen. So you were just exaggerating, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not exaggerating. By the word "every citizen" I mean elderly people and young people, but those citizens who had some friendly relations with Serbian nationals tried to find a way to help us not to leave the place. It's absurd to say that 3.000 inhabitants could go to Serb families to ask them to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you say things like "every person" and "every citizen" and "everyone," we should understand that you really don't mean that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to stop you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness? We should not take that as literal when you say "everyone, every person, every citizen"?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every citizen in the literal sense of the word, but many citizens, the people in the village, those who, as I said, good relations with Serbs in authority not with just any Serb. Because it's absurd to say every citizen and every Serbian family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you said that, so what you said is absurd; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean some citizens or many citizens or we citizens tried our best to contact people with authority, and I showed you that we contacted Vlado, that we tried to reach Bora, to meet the chief of the police, Peric --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us all about this, we don't need to hear it again, and we're trying to finish this up. I'm going to go on to a different subject. Let me ask you, as we complete this process, could you please try to be more precise. And when you don't mean every, don't say "every," okay because I wouldn't want you to be absurd again. You talked about April 13th of 1999 when three soldiers came to your mother's house looking for you. And with regard to those three soldiers, yesterday you told us that they said to you, and you used the words "they said," which probably is not the case. "It's good that we found you. We apologise" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have questions without the commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Ackerman, I think the tiredness is beginning to show, so let's try confine this to questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
