utterances.text: You claim they said to you: "It's good that we found you. We apologise, but an order had come from the supreme staff in Belgrade. Prilepnica must be evacuated." That's page 35, line 16. Now, you didn't tell this to Ms. Driguet when she interviewed you in April of 1999, did you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the name and last name of the first and the last -- second officer in every one of my statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is that they said to you: "We apologise, but an order came from the supreme staff in Belgrade. Prilepnica must be evacuated." That's not what you told Ms. Driguet when she interviewed you in 1999, is it? You didn't tell her that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told her the first and the last names of both officers, and I did this -- I told this to everyone that asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Shaqiri, is not about the names of the officers; it's about the fact of an order from the supreme staff and that these soldiers told you that they had such an order. And the question is why you did not tell that to Ms. Driguet, who interviewed you on the 25th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't mention the word "soldier." When my sister-in-law came and she told us that the soldiers entered the courtyard, I went out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop, there must be something wrong with the translation that's going through --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Must be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because I don't think you're being -- you possibly could have misunderstood that three times. So let me try to spell out in words that no one can misinterpret or misunderstand. What Mr. Ackerman wants to know is why you did not tell Ms. Driguet, who interviewed you on the 25th of April, that the three army officers who came looking for you on the 13th of April told you that they had an order from the supreme staff in Belgrade that Prilepnica must be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Driguet asked me and I answered her questions. She told me: Don't answer what I am not asking you. So whatever she asked me, I answered. In this case, she may not have asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when we started this process this morning and when we started this process yesterday, I said: Answer the questions I ask you, nothing more. Don't volunteer anything. Just listen to my questions; if you don't understand them -- answer them. And throughout the day you've given information beyond what I've asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, we're now into an area that is far from clear. I don't accept that this has been evidence given in the form in which we've had evidence from a number of other witnesses. This is not a witness who embarks upon his life story every time a simple question is asked of him. I think you're being less than fair to him with that characterisation of his evidence, and therefore let's move to more precise questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour, and I will come back to that because I can make it clearer, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you did tell Ms. Driguet in 1999 that this person Djilas, who was one of these three men, told you that they had orders from the regular Serbian army to empty the village, that nobody was to remain, nobody at all. Do you remember that that's what you told her and not something from the supreme staff in Belgrade? It's on page 5, paragraph 10 of that statement that you have in front of you. Page 5, paragraph 10, if you just count from the top, get down to paragraph 10, you'll find it. It could be paragraph 9. It's 9 or 10, depending on how you count them. Let me know when you find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, but the translation is wrong, entirely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, 1999, it was a Tuesday -- in the morning around 11.30, some soldiers, some soldiers -- two officers, there is a mistake here -- came to my mother's house. They entered my mother's house. I was there. And asked if the imam was there. They asked to see me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need to hear again what you told us yesterday was the evidence. All that we are looking at the moment, Mr. Shaqiri, is what was said before and how that compares with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's reading the wrong paragraph, Your Honour, he's reading paragraph 7 instead of 9. All he has to go is go down two paragraphs and he'll find the language about it being the regular Serbian army, as opposed to supreme staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I must say, I was assuming that he was at the right paragraph. I don't see any reason would we shouldn't, and he's saying that the translation was entirely wrong is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he's reading from paragraph 7 and I told him to look at paragraph 10. So I don't care if it's wrong at paragraph 7, and this is in the Serbo-Croat, Your Honour, not in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which paragraph on the English version should I be looking at then? I'm looking at paragraph 49 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's page 5, paragraph 49 if they are numbered the same way mine are, Your Honour, I think they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, 49. Now, Mr. Shaqiri, in English the paragraph we are looking at begins: "Djilas was the one who talked ... " and it then says: "He told me he had orders from the regular Serbian army to empty the village."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct. Yes, it's correct. This version is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing we can conclude from that is that Djilas was not a member of the regular Serbian army because he's referring to orders that he got from the regular Serbian army; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a lawyer, a judge. He conveyed - at least this is what he said - that we represent the regular Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this order that the village was to be emptied included everyone in the village, the Albanian people, the Serb people, the Roma people, everybody; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that it's permissible under the law of the Federal Republic of Serbia -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time for a military commander to order the evacuation of a village in the time of war? Were you aware that that was permissible?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but that was the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Djilas also told you on that day, as you were talking with him, that the soldiers had -- that ordered you to leave on the 6th of April were paramilitary. You told us that yesterday at page 38, line 4. And then you said: "It didn't even occur to me to call them paramilitary army. This is what Djilas called them, this formation of the 6th of April." True?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a Crisis Staff that existed in Gjilan at this time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it perhaps a Crisis Staff you were talking about yesterday when you mentioned that Bora Denic was a member of the military staff in Gjilan, would that have been the Crisis Staff in Gjilan, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- sorry. I want to be clear about one thing, though. Mr. Ackerman appears to have moved away from the reference that you made yesterday to being told that there were orders from the supreme staff in Belgrade. Now, how does that relate to the paragraph that you read, referring to Djilas having orders from the regular Serbian army to empty the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what he said in my presence, that the order has come from Belgrade, from the supreme staff, for Prilepnica to be evacuated. If necessary, I can say it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really hesitate to try to do anything more with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 21, line 1 of the transcript from yesterday there's a quote from you I want to ask you about. You said: "The Yugoslav army was there in our country." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean? For what period of time are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the period of time in April of 1999 that we've been talking about the whole time you've been here. And you said with regard to that period of time: "The Yugoslav army was there in our country." I want to know what you mean by "our country."

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "our country" I mean that the army was in our municipality, not in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you referred to your municipality as being a country; is that what you're saying to me?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A municipality is a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- and then you're not answering the question I asked you. I asked you what you meant when you said: "The ... army was in our country." When you used the words "our country," what were you referring to, what country?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any country on my mind. My answers refer to 6th, 13th, and 14th of April, and as for the army, it was the Yugoslav army or the Serbian-Montenegrin army, whatever you call it. They were always in Gjilan. They travelled through Gjilan to come from Serbia to Kosova. And at that time our part, the Anamorava part, had no problems whatsoever with the army. And if anyone tells you that they had an incident with the army - and I mean the Yugoslav army because I've served there - if I used the word "Yugoslav" then I apologise, but this is what I learned at school. And when I learnt it, it was Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not quarrelling with you about that. The place you were living at the time, your municipality, your village was in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April of 1999, wasn't it? There was no Serbia and Montenegro yet; it was still the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. For me, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm back now to page 40, line 23 of your testimony yesterday, and this is now back on the 13th of April and maybe the 14th, but I think it's the 13th. You told us that: "The army encircled the village because some villagers began to flee and now that they'd encircled the village, nobody could leave." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If there's an order to completely empty the village, why are they circling the village to keep people from leaving the village? That makes no sense to me. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, on the 6th of April we fled from the opposite side of the village in the direction of Bujanovc. We had escaped danger once. If it wasn't for the army, we wouldn't have moved out. This order was for the next day, for the 14th, not for the 13th. According to the order, we were supposed to leave on the 14th under escort. We didn't know at the time whether we would be escorted by the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you had actually requested an escort, hadn't you? You were saying you weren't going to leave unless you had an escort?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said you really didn't care -- you didn't care whether it was police or army that escorted you, as long as you had an escort?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I would not take the responsibility to lead the villagers. This is what I said, and I can repeat it now that it really didn't matter who would escort us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. So on the 14th of April, as you said in your 2001 statement, about 3.000 people left the village that day in cars and tractors and had a police escort; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's one thing I'm a little bit curious about and I don't want to spend much time on this, but on the 28th of August when you talked to the Prosecutor about your various statements, what they call their supplement, paragraph 22 of that document, you said you got your escort and you heard a person over the radio ask if you needed fuel or a bus. And you said that you declined any assistance other than the escort. The other assistance offered you was fuel and a bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't accept it. I just didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there any other assistance offered you besides the fuel and the bus?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked if there was a need for such an assistance, and I replied that there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, my question was: Did they offer you any other assistance besides a bus and some fuel?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this same supplement you apparently told the Prosecutor this that at one point you told the escort that you weren't going to go and that a police officer you knew advised you that you should go with him and that you believe this was done to protect the villagers and Mr. Shaqiri, and you, and that officer said that he was ordered to escort you and seemed apologetic for having to do it. Is that what you told somebody from the OTP on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an officer, but a traffic policeman. I never said his name before, but I mentioned it yesterday that this very same policeman works now with the police force in Kosova, SHPK. He works in Kamenica. He is a family person, he's an honourable citizen, and he really felt apologetic that he had to escort us and do this. He is a traffic policeman from Ranilluga. Maybe I wouldn't have mentioned it even today, but you forced me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I hope I didn't force you to do anything today, but let me ask you this: What I don't understand is --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I don't understand is if you request an escort, why would that escort apologise for doing what you asked?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote: "Hoxha, I apologise. You have to come with me." Now, whether it is apologetic or not, this is what he said. I've quoted his words. I've known him for a long time and I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, this next question I want to try to get through quickly; I hope we can do that. Yesterday you told Mr. Hannis that when you -- when you had left your village and went up toward that well that you were going to to meet the escort, that you met another group of people that were coming from Kosac village. And yesterday you told us that there were 3 or 400 people, and you even said up to 600 people, and that's page 41, line 16. In the statement you gave in 1999 you said there were 900 people in that group. And I only want to know which of those is the most accurate number, the one you gave in 1999 or the one you gave us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something here. There are 300 or 400 in Kosac, but I've also mentioned Kmetofc village when I was asked and other villages as well. I have said that there are 900 and even 1.000 now. At that time, in that convoy, there were 300 or 400. There were other people who were also ordered to move. Approximately 3.000 from Prilepnica and around 1.000 from other villages. I don't know what you got from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I really do need now to read to you what you said in your statement to the OTP in April of 1999, and you should be able to find it, I think. Let me see if I can find where it was now. In the English it's paragraph 54. You said they -- you went in the direction of Kosaca. It's paragraph 2 on page 6 in what you have in front of you. And then you said this, you referred to Kosaca and then you said: "The inhabitants of that village, some 900 people, were waiting for me there, having received the same orders to leave their village." So you're clearly referring only to the people from Kosaca at that point, and the question I'm trying to ask and trying to get an answer to is: Why did you say 3 to 400, up to 600, yesterday and say 900 at that time and which of those is more accurate?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated yesterday and what I stated that time in my statement I want to emphasise again, that there are other houses that are in Kosac village. I haven't counted the inhabitants. The village Kosac proper has about 300 to 400 inhabitants, and now as to how many were there in the column, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm going to go on now. You don't know. Yesterday, page 42, line 2, you were asked this by Mr. Hannis: "After the villagers from Kosac joined your convoy, where did you go?" And you said this: "We walked for another 50 or 60 metres to the main road." Now, my question is: Why were you walking? You were in a car, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So why did you say you walked for 50 or 60 metres to the main road?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not on foot. We were with vehicles. The convoy was walking, not us. The convoy was walking for some 50 or 60 metres up to the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you got to this location at the well, you told us yesterday that you had met a reservist who you told you were waiting for an escort. And you told us yesterday that he offended you. Can you tell us what he did to offend you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the crossroads. While the column was moving, I was at the head of the column. I stopped, the column stopped as well. And in a strict voice he said -- I will mention some words, not all of them, because they are offensive --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if it's offensive words --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: "Why did you stop here?" And cursed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's offensive words, I'm really not interested in hearing them. I'm just wondering if he'd done anything beyond that. All right. Let me go to another question. At page 42 of your testimony yesterday, Mr. Hannis asked you this question, and please pay attention to the question that he asked you. It was: "After the villagers from Kosac joined your convoy, where did you go?" Don't answer that, but I just want to point out that's the question you were asked. Okay? Now, under the heading of: I only answer the questions that I'm asked, in the process of answering that question you said, "I want to mention a small detail here. A black Mercedes came there. It belonged to high-ranking officers. There were four persons in that Mercedes. I would say all of them were generals. They stopped the Mercedes. I was 5 or 6 metres far from this vehicle speaking to this reservist military person." Now, you had never mentioned that in any statement that you ever gave before, had you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you first tell the Office of the Prosecutor about this black Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, because I didn't recognise this -- these officers. They were there at ten past 8.00 at the well. They spoke for a minute or two with the same soldier who had the radio, and then they proceeded with their journey. In my statement, I've always answered questions that were put to me; I did not answer things that were not asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's not the way it happened yesterday, is it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. While we were talking about the uniform of this soldier who was there, so we were speaking for quite some time, and I just remembered the moment when they came and when they spoke with these officers. If this thing with this soldier didn't go on for a long time, maybe I wouldn't have remembered. They just came there shortly and left. Officers and soldiers, they always moved up and down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you thought in this Mercedes there were generals, four generals. You still want to maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For me, high-ranking officers are those who are from major and above and who have these gold-colour stripes. They have them on their shoulders and on their caps. So on basis of these stripes, they must have been lieutenant-colonels or colonels and above, not below.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about soldiers that were not part of the regular army that would go around in private cars. Don't you suspect that's what this was, some soldiers that were not part of the regular army going around in a private car?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked, according to you: What is the difference between a regular army and an army that is not a regular one? And my reply was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now we're -- you're going off somewhere we don't need to go.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it's: Yes, because those who were driving private cars, at least to me, are not regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And one thing that would help you in understanding that was if these really had been high-ranking regular army generals or in that -- of that ilk, there would have been quite a lot of security with them, soldiers with guns and -- securing the group; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need just a second. My computer keeps shutting off in the midst of these things, and so I can't see the transcript anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that allows me to ask Mr. Shaqiri what he's really saying now. Are you saying that these were persons who were not in the regular army because it was a private car? Or what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing military uniforms. They had golden ribbons on their caps, and they had military ranks. They were in a black Mercedes. Now, I don't know whether it was a military vehicle or a private one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this was -- this was during a time, was it not, when NATO was still involved in bombing Serbia, Yugoslavia, Kosovo, hundreds and hundreds of NATO aircraft were in the air; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope we're not exaggerating there, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hundreds and hundreds of aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that they flew many, many missions, but are we talking about hundreds and hundreds of aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many of them were in the air at any one time, Your Honour. I know there was a lot involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to trust my memory on the number of missions, but it was well of 7.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I understand that, but that's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you divide that by the number of days involved, that's a number of airplanes in the air every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm on page 43 of your transcript, and this is when we got in -- in all of this confusion yesterday about uniforms, and I -- I want to try to clear this up if I can, and I probably can't, but I want to try. You were asked about this officer who offended you and you said about that officer at line 4: "He was a reservist in the police force. He was wearing a dark blue uniform, a winter uniform, that is, heavy clothes." "Q. How did you know he was a reservist as opposed to a regular policeman?" "A. Because I used to wear the same uniform for 15 years." Now, I think where we got yesterday with you was you really didn't wear that same uniform for 15 years; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "the same uniform," but I said I kept the uniform of a reservist for 15 years. This is what I'm saying. Maybe it was wrongly translated. I said mine was olive-green, SMB, olive-green-grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the position you're taking today is that the translators in this courtroom or the court reporter who wrote down what she heard wrote it down wrong and you didn't say: I used to wear the same uniform for 15 years. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would indicate yesterday during the break I heard from a sensitive source on the other side of the room who I can't name indicated that he heard in the translation there was a mistake regarding whether or not there was a blue uniform or a green uniform. I don't speak Serbian or Albanian, so I can't speak to that, but that was the information I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the witness this then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness made it clear yesterday that the uniform he had was green; that wasn't the issue I don't think, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, apparently from what Mr. Hannis has said today, what was wrongly translated was the word "blue." But when he answered he was wearing a dark blue uniform, that he didn't say "blue" that he said "green." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on, show me that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, in yesterday -- you're talking about -- you haven't got the updated one, sorry. Just give me a second. Mr. Hannis, are you talking about the passage at 28:07, line 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was looking at line 18 and 19, yes, Your Honour. I think that's my understanding where it was apparently translated in the transcript his answer was that reservist was wearing a blue uniform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just, you don't need to read this out. Just let me see. Now, Mr. Shaqiri, the reservist that you say offended you at the crossroads was a reservist in which force, the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. His uniform was blue and he was communicating by radio with the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just stop there. So you're clear the uniform was blue; that's exactly what the transcript says. So there isn't a mistake there. Now, what colour was your uniform that you either kept or wore for 15 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SMB, or olive-green -- dark olive- green.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I stop there. You mentioned yesterday your brother. What uniform did he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had the uniform of a reservist, too, blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Blue, yeah. Now, Mr. Ackerman, that confirms what was said yesterday about colours. You can proceed from there, but bear in mind that intertwined into all this was a reference to the brother's uniform also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Judge just asked you what service this person was from that offended you. You told the Judge you didn't know. Yesterday you told the Judge in response to a question from Mr. Hannis that he was a reservist in the police force. Now, which is true? Do you not know or was he a reservist in the police force?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it yesterday. According to the uniform, I mentioned the military police, not the police, at least that was my impression. I don't know whether that is correct. So you must add military police, not only police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you -- having been in the army, you must know that the military police wore regular army uniforms with white belts. You must know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they are traffic police, while the other police, at least in my time, had this kind of uniform, that is, military police. They usually had motor-bikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Military police wore regular army uniforms with white belts, didn't they, not blue uniforms? If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my time I'm talking - I did my military service in 1968/1969 - the ones that wore white belts were military traffic police. We call them saobracajci , military traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in 1968 and 1969 when you served, the military police wore blue uniforms; is that what you're saying? That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long time has passed. At that time the soldiers who were serving within the barracks used the same uniform; outside the barracks they used this white belt. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're going to move on. At Kllokot -- you went to Kllokot in Vitina municipality. You went through a check-point there which you said had police and military. And you said this: "It would have been impossible to pass through if we had not been escorted." That's in your statement of June 2001 at page 4, paragraph 14. How did you come up with such a conclusion, that if you hadn't had an escort you wouldn't be able to pass through that check-point in Kllokot? Nothing had happened to you the whole time on the trip, had it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a check-point where we were greatly insulted, pointed guns at. Hadn't he had any escort, probably they might have stopped the convoy and we might have fared worse, but fortunately for us we didn't have any problems thanks to Jova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said there were police and military at that check-point, and you were being escorted by police so I take it you had no concern about the police; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police escorted us, that's a fact. And there, there were people who had both military and police uniforms, but they insulted us on the way, not only us at the head of the convoy, but other people as well. These were people who maintained a savage attitude towards the convoy, using all sorts of insulting word and threats. And based on this, I came to the conclusion that hadn't we had an escort -- maybe, I'm saying "maybe," - we would have fared worse. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, "maybe" makes sense to me. What you said was: "It would have been impossible to pass through had we not had an escort." That's different from maybe, isn't it? I'm going to move on. As you neared the border, you came to a spring, and it was there that you encountered another officer that asked you where you were coming from and why; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a check-point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this officer asked you where you were coming from and why, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and "Why are you leaving," he said to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. He obviously had no idea that your group was coming to his check-point. He was surprised that you'd arrived there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was at that point that this soldier started hitting you and was stopped by the policeman Jova.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, sir, he was the officer I talked to, and he ordered me to get off my car and line up the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. My question is really simple. Jova stopped this soldier from hitting you, this person from hitting you; right?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the officer there apologised to you for what that person had done in hitting you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were angry about that and didn't accept his apology and sort of made a deal with him that you wouldn't be searched or anything like that, and you honoured the deal and he honoured the deal and you went on your way without being searched; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of June 2001 you -- you told Ms. Murtagh who was interviewing you at that time that you later heard that the rest of the people were actually searched. And then on the 28th of August when you talked to the attorneys here at the Tribunal, you said that was not the case, that they were not searched. Now, did you learn something between those two statements to cause you to change your mind?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to make an explanation here. The first 50 vehicles were escorted up to the meadow or at the border police until he was not there. When he was not there, a military patrol wanted to search or to loot them. And when he came back, he engaged in a conversation with him. And the inhabitants told me this: This control -- this column is moving without any control. So we moved without being searched up to the border. I mean thanks to that intervention by that officer, we were not searched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, the question you're being asked is: Why did you say in a statement in 2001 that everyone else was searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a mistake, Your Honour. Those who remained at the check-point -- the soldiers that came in the meantime wanted to search them, but at that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't want to hear the explanation of the event again. What we want to try and understand is why you give two completely different versions on two separate occasions; that's really what this is about. Now, why did you -- you're indicating now that in 2001 you didn't say that everyone else was searched. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not clear. I'm sorry. I'm not clear from the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, who has the benefit of seeing your statement in 2001, which I don't have, says that in that statement you claimed that while you weren't searched, for reasons you've just explained, nevertheless everyone else in the convoy was searched. Now, why did you say that in -- in the year 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say this in 2001; I never said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you then any idea how it might have got into your statement, which was read back to you as I understand it in your own language, and I think this particular statement was also signed on each page? Is that -- is this the one that -- this statement signed on every page, read back to you in your own language and has these words in it. So how -- can you help us to understand how that got into the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not possible. Can you give me the Albanian version of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, I don't even have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can do it, Your Honour. It is Exhibit 4D6, and if Exhibit 4D6 could be put up on the monitors, the Albanian version for the witness, the English for Your Honours. And in the English, at least, it's the -- it's the next-to-the-last paragraph on page 6. I have no idea where it is in Albanian; I know where it is in B/C/S. I see the first page on the screen. We just need to go to page 6 and we'll be there. In the Albanian it will be the final paragraph on page 7, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Serbian it's on page 6, paragraph 3, but I don't have page 6 on my monitor yet. I still have page 1. I see, it's on this monitor over here. But it's the page before that one. It says "page 6" on the bottom. You need to go right to the bottom of that page, so go back a page. Okay. Well, now we got --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, it's on your screen now in Serbian, and I don't know what the Judges have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I thought we were looking for an Albanian version. Is there no such thing in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is. It's one of the documents. It's in there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the trouble is -- I know that this has arisen in the course of the cross-examination, but it's important to try to have page references for the exhibit. And it won't be page 6 of the Albanian version that you're -- you need to have, it's the page number that page 6 of the Albanian version happens to have in the system that you need to know. And there are three of you sitting at that table and one of you doing some work, and the other two, I think, could perhaps being busily putting together for you, Mr. Ackerman, an indication what these page numbers might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy that we could hand the witness of the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be next to the last paragraph. The Albanian version is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that in Albanian it's page 7, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 7, last paragraph, that's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you're looking for is the last sentence of that paragraph: "I later heard that the rest of the people who were left were actually searched by the other soldiers." That's what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Albanian it's not as you are saying, and I will read it word for word, if it's necessary and the interpreter will translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please read it word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Another officer and Jova took away the soldier who had hit me. The officer came and apologised on behalf of the soldier, but I did not accept the apology. I said: He's your soldier. You are responsible for him. I said: You should be ashamed of yourself for not being able to take responsibility for a soldier while I take responsibility for 3.000 people. I said: You may do what you like, but you are not human beings. I was very upset, and as a result of the quarrel with the officer we were not searched, nor was there any money taken from us. The military officer promised they would not search the convoy. I want to convince you this is not my mistake, he said. This officer then escorted me to the border with 50 vehicles. Each group of 50 vehicles was escorted to the border by other officers. It was 4 to 5 kilometres away. Later I heard that" -- doesn't matter then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the next bit that does matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I later heard that the rest of the people in fact were searched by the other soldiers, even though the officer had promised me that they would not be searched."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the part we want to know about. Why is that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why it is there. I was informed, Your Honour, that the soldiers went there to search the convoy, but thanks to the intervention -- I might have said the opposite, but I didn't want to say untruths. I have taken the oath to say the truth. So thanks to the intervention by the Serbian officer, they were not searched. So something is wrong here. Then later I heard from the others that some soldiers went to the convoy to search them, but once the officer arrived - which is not here - he took away the soldiers and my people was not searched. And I say this in full responsibility here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think I'll not pursue that any further. You eventually returned to your village after the NATO intervention ended. You told us yesterday that you found the village burnt to the ground, destroyed, looted, including the mosque, and that was at page 57 of the transcript, line 6. In your correction statement of 2002, that's 5 February 2002, the one where you made corrections with Jan Pfundheller, what you said to Mr. Pfundheller about what happened in your village, you said when you returned to Prilepnica 123 of the 300 houses had been burned and all had been looted. Now, which one is it? Was the village burnt to the ground or were 123 of 300 houses burned?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire village was destroyed and burned to the ground are 123 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you count this number of houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there is proof from the municipality. They have carried out in a professional way the calculation of all the damage caused by the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you tell us yesterday the village had been burnt to the ground - those were your words - when the truth was that 123 of 300 houses, less than half, had actually been burned? Why did you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted. The village was burned, it was looted, it was fully destroyed, while 123 houses were totally burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're saying where the transcript says from yesterday that you said the village was burnt to the ground, that that's not true, that that's not what you said?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, there were houses that were not burned, but they were damaged, demolished --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you need to understand what I'm asking you. There's no doubt that what you said at page 57, line 6, that you told Mr. Hannis you found the village burnt to the ground. Now, my question is: Are you saying now that you didn't say that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "burnt to the ground." I mentioned the figure 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this is a mistake of interpretation in the transcript yesterday? They got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you either said it was burnt to the ground or you didn't; which is it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said "to the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have an audio recording of your testimony yesterday. We can check it, you know. Do you want us to check it, see if you're telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this has gone beyond the point of being helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree, Mr. Hannis. I am finding it helpful. In fact, I have noted to make exactly the check that Mr. Ackerman is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You think we need to do that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what you're saying, then I will withdraw that answer because the entire village was not burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What about the Roma houses in your village, were they burned to the ground?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned, they were also burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What about the Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for that particular moment, but later on they were burned as well. Now, whether they were all burned or not, I don't know. I can say that they were burned, but whether now 100 per cent were burned, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there a church in Prilepnica, Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This person that you speak of in your statement of 25 April 1999, this Goran Denic who has three names, did you know that this person was later arrested along with a group of other civilians for setting the fires in Prilepnica? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one last question for you. Yesterday at the very beginning of your testimony you were asked by Mr. Hannis about your military service and you said: "I was in the front line, the 20th Guards Platoon." What front line was there in 1968? There wasn't any war going on in 1968, was there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a mistake. I will say it again in the original, in Serbian. I was in the 20th Guards Regiment in the first echelon in wartime establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So "first echelon" was misinterpreted to "front line"; is that what you're saying? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's for him to Judge, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't either, Your Honour. I've got no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's time for another break, and we will -- we'll resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Reluctantly I do, Your Honour. At page 27 of the transcript today Mr. Ackerman was asking the witness about a handwritten statement that he mentioned having given to a lawyer named Masar Morina from Gjilan. When we heard that information, we started searching. I have discovered that handwritten statement and an English translation, which based on our search has not been disclosed to the Defence prior to today. During the break, I handed them a hard copy of the handwritten statement in Albanian and the English translation. It appears there is also a four-page interview form that is related to that as well and I bring it to your attention and the Defence's attention for whatever action you deem it appropriate at this time. I thought I should bring it to your attention as early as possible so we can figure out the best way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you yourself been able to make an assessment on whether it has any impact on the evidence we've heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I can indicate to you that in the sense of being an additional statement about the same events, it has many parts that are similar or identical, but it also has some parts that are different and would be the kind of thing that Defence may want to cross-examine about. At some point I would argue that some of it has a cumulative effect, but they are in a better position to assess that. It has a couple of things that he told someone at some time that did not appear in any of the other statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Ackerman, first, what do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You want to hear from Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would rather hear from Mr. Ackerman since he has concluded his cross-examination and what impact it might have on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't had a chance to read it. It's 17 single-spaced pages in the English, and I haven't been given this interview form that Mr. Hannis just mentioned, the four-page interview form, I have no idea what that is. I certainly don't want to close my cross-examination now. I want to be able to continue tomorrow if there's something in this that I think merits additional questioning. I must say that I'm quite distressed that this would come to us this late, it should have come to us a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your distress is matched by that of Mr. Hannis, though, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that, I think it is. I'm certainly not suggesting it's anything deliberate on the part of the Prosecution that we didn't get it. But having just gotten it we have to have a chance to consider it. If I had not cross-examined yet, I would want you to give me the evening to look at it because it could affect what I have asked or would ask. So I think it's a big wrench thrown into this witness's testimony that we need to deal with in a reasonable way and I think a reasonable way is to perhaps defer any cross until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, how are you placed by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Let me not repeat Mr. Ackerman's arguments. I also need time to familiarise myself with this precisely because of the fact that I will have to cross-examine now, and I don't really want to repeat everything that Mr. Ackerman has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sepenuk, are you adding to this or are you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I just had an inquiry, Your Honour. Mr. Hannis said -- we have this statement he described but he said there's also a four-page statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you should be given that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an interview form that seems to be related to the actual statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's entitled: A questionnaire of war crimes committed in Kosovo of which this witness was an interviewee. I just received the copies now that I'll hand to the Defence right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it related to the handwritten statement or is it actually separate from it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did say it was related, but I mean at first blush it may not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can't say, Your Honour, because the named interviewer is described as a member of the central war crimes commission in charge of gathering the evidence, and that is the group, as I understand it, that Mr. Morina was attached to. So it appeared to be related in that sense. But I can't tell if it was done contemporaneous with or prior to or after the handwritten statement was composed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, can you help me on how this situation could arise or do you need to investigate that further?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to do some further investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No one's suggesting anything other than an accident at the moment, but even then I think we have to try and learn from the experience to try and avoid any repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you know, for ought yet seen, as we say, I better speak simple English, I suppose. No one speaks simpler English than I do. Well, it's been translated pretty well. For ought yet seen, there may be some objection taken, so it would, I think, be necessary for you to investigate and explain tomorrow what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I need to know for my own purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Shaqiri, we're -- we're grateful to you for alerting us all to the fact that there was another statement which you had written. That statement has now been traced, but it was not available to the lawyers representing the accused in this case until 15 minutes ago. And in these circumstances, it is necessary for us to give them time to read the statement and there's also some additional information, so that they can adjust, if appropriate, the questions that they will ask you. Indeed, it may simplify your evidence or it may complicate it. No one can tell at the moment. We've decided that in these circumstances the best thing is now to adjourn until tomorrow. So that completes your evidence for today, but you will be required to return here again tomorrow at 2.15, same arrangement as today. Meanwhile, again, it's very important that you have no discussion with anyone about any part of your evidence or the evidence you will give in the court. So we'll see you tomorrow at 2.15. Meanwhile, we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to not use up the time tomorrow, there's a bit of business we can do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we need Mr. Shaqiri?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We certainly don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're free to leave the courtroom, Mr. Shaqiri. We can deal with things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This will take seconds not minutes, but I forgot to do it at the beginning of my cross. I want to move the admission of Exhibits 4D4 4D5, 4D6, 4D8, and 4D9. Those are the statements from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's noted. Thank you. Anybody got anything else to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a quick question, has the exhibit I believe it was Prosecution Exhibit 2288, I guess they're calling it the OSCE report, has it been introduced into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It just was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay, that answers my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one other thing I think just to tidy the record completely is to note that IC29 is actually 4D4. Is that -- sorry, IC32 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually 4D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the 25th of April statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it's 4D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there a mechanism for striking an exhibit? So we can strike-out IC32 and that won't cause confusion when you give another exhibit the same number? No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be available for the next IC document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That could be given to the next IC --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem with that is if a future appellate lawyer is looking at the transcript and sees IC32 and goes and looks at it, it's not going to be the exhibit the transcript is talking about. So you better leave it as is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm satisfied that the transcript that we are now participating in creating clarifies the position sufficiently for any future reader to see that the reference to IC32 earlier today should be substituted by a reference to 4D4, which is the same exhibit which already was part of the e-court library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there any possibility, just so it becomes real clear, that those who are in charge of updating this transcript, this is a raw version, can actually replace IC32 with 4D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the answer to that is there is no point in doing it. I think from memory it was only referred to by the registrar giving it that number. And there was no question that was asked: Can you look at IC32. Otherwise I would agree with you, that might be a way of doing it. I think the way we've just done it is the way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have done an enormous work of appellate work in my time and one of the greatest frustrations is finding a reference to a document which is not the document that you expect it to be and that can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure the appellate court is going to enjoy reading our exchange, and that will make them particularly alert to this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect so, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, but would you just allow me a minute. I just need to clarify something. In this specific case it was my understanding - and I hope that I can receive an explanation now - witness statement, for example like in this case, once it's in the system and once it is put to the witness, is it not automatically included in the evidence or do we have to identify it with a number every time and do we have to tender it every time? We don't want to take up time. You see what I'm saying? So in the future we'd like to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're absolutely right in what you say and the practice has been to identify the document by referring to its number so that it can then be placed on the screen. And once the witness is asked about it, then it's part of the record to the extent that it has been dealt with in the course of the proceedings. The only situation where it seems to me necessary to deal with it in a rather separate way is, for example, when Mr. Ackerman invited us to give consideration to the whole terms of a statement that he decided not to cross-examine a witness on in detail and he was making it clear that he was inviting us to consider that for all its contents to be compared against the evidence of the accused -- of the witness in court. And there -- in that sort of situation, the position should be made clear. But I gather that those that administer the system feel more comfortable when the word "tender" at least has been used and any doubt -- any lingering doubt is removed. But you can take it from the Bench that we will consider every exhibit that is referred to in any context in the evidence, to the extent that it is relevant to the evidence presented to us, so to that extent it's automatically a part of the record whenever it's introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for this explanation and thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you may be a bit premature. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the last word. When I was referring to a potential future appeal, you must understand I was referring to an appeal by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But with permission of the chair, I wish to add one thing, Mr. Ackerman, and that is, frustration is a part of your profession and ours, too, so when you talk of that you should always accept it. It is a profession of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there we are. With great regret, we adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
